extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary writers, and students of literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for creating and judging poetry and poetic prose, with emphasis on natural expression, adequacy of form, attention to Nature, and formation of an individual style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of vehicle/form
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetic vehicle must be adequate to the scale and pitch of the work; some forms (e.g., the couplet) may be admirable for certain uses but 'inadequate' for continuous use in higher-pitched poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by comparison: Lucretius has an adequate vehicle for his poem on Nature, while Pope's couplet is inadequate for sustained didactic or high poetic pitch. The vehicle can compensate or hamper even a great genius: 'Of such avail is the superior adequacy of the vehicle used to compensate even an inferiority of genius in the user!' Choose a form that sustains the work's demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretative faculty and rendering of Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A great writer shows 'a truly interpretative faculty; the most profound and delicate sense of the life of Nature, and the most exquisite felicity in finding expressions to render that sense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value prose/poetry that not only perceives Nature but interprets and renders it with felicitous expression (examples in Guérin's journals and the Centaur). This faculty distinguishes memorable poetic prose from mere description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant observation of Nature's smallest details
rubrics_metrics.description: Be constantly observing Nature in her smallest details, and then write as the current of your thoughts guides you; — that is all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule for composing: sustained, attentive observation supplies material and tone (supported by Guérin's journal entries on spring, primroses, green, sea). Emphasizes immediacy and fidelity to perception rather than abstract theorizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form a style of your own; avoid sing-song and imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Form for yourself a style of your own; 'Your verse is too sing-song; it does not talk enough.' Study masters but do not adopt any master's manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the language 'by attentive reading, making it your care to remark constructions, turns of expression, delicacies of style,' but 'use it each in our own fashion.' The goal is a personal, talking voice rather than tuneful but empty cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'literature facile' and premature, superficial romanticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the facile, prematurely-blown literature that yields ephemeral blossoms and little lasting fruit: 'that youthful literature which has put forth all its blossom prematurely... will most likely reduce to a handful of grains the harvest of our age.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipattern: popular, novelty-chasing writing whose reputation is fleeting. Aim instead for depth and maturity that produce lasting value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work should nourish the human soul ('hidden manna')
rubrics_metrics.description: A worthy work contains 'hidden manna' — 'sweet and wholesome thoughts which nourish the human soul and refresh it when it is weary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for lasting literary merit: does the work provide sustenance to readers' inner life? Avoid merely fashionable cleverness that lacks sustaining thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of reading and multilingual acquaintance
rubrics_metrics.description: Wide and serious reading across languages and traditions (e.g., Bernardin de St. Pierre, Chateaubriand, Lamartine, Hugo, Homer, Dante, Shakespeare, Milton, Goethe) sharpens literary tact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guérin's reading in French, Greek, and English is cited as contributing to his 'beautiful and true' literary tact. Familiarity with originals and diverse models informs precision and depth without forcing imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance freedom from rules with precision of judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: While freeing oneself from the bondage of forms and rules, one must still 'mark with perfect precision the faults' of inferior literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate imaginative freedom but retain the critical precision to detect and avoid faults (precision in style, diction, and judgement complements creative liberty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make verse 'talk'—prioritize speech-like clarity over mere music
rubrics_metrics.description: Verse should 'talk' — be communicative and alive — rather than be merely 'sing-song.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer immediacy and conversational vitality in poetic diction so that poems feel like living speech, not ornamental sound alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek natural, happy, and true expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal mode of expression is 'the most natural, happy, and true.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than forced mannerisms or slavish adherence to trends, aim for an expression that feels inevitable and true to the writer's sensibility and to the material.
